summary: The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery. It models the Solar System. It was built in the 2nd century BC. It is the oldest known analogue computer. It predicted astronomical positions and eclipses decades ahead. It also tracked the cycle of the ancient Olympic Games. It was recovered in 1901 from a Roman cargo shipwreck. The wreck lies off the Greek island of Antikythera. The ship sank around 70 to 60 BC. In 1902, Valerios and Spyridon Stais noticed a gear in it. It survives as 82 fragments in Athens' National Archaeological Museum. Scans in 2005 suggest 35 meshing bronze gears. They followed the Sun and Moon through the zodiac. They also predicted eclipses and modelled the Moon's irregular orbit. It uses Hipparchus' theory of the Moon's motion. Hipparchus may have helped design it. Some speculate it also calculated the five classical planets. Its dating is disputed, from about 205 BC to 87 BC. Proposed origins include Corinth's colonies, Pergamon and Rhodes. Machines this complex appeared again only in 14th-century Europe.
